talks.title: BSidesSF 2022 - Keynote: We Need More Mediocre Security Engineers (Jackie Bow)
talks.teaser: Examines BSidesSF 2022 - Keynote: teams Need More Mediocre Security Engineers (Jackie Bow) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Jackie Bow, Head of Threat Detection and Response at Asana and former security engineer at Facebook, Patreon, and the U.S. Government, delivers the opening keynote at BSidesSF 2022. Bow challenges the industry's obsession with "10x rockstar" engineers, advocating for a cultural redefinition of "mediocrity" centered on realistic human performance, psychological safety, and sustainable engineering practices. She analyzes the systemic flaws in cybersecurity recruitment and interviewing that perpetuate a 600,000-person labor shortage, offering practical strategies to diversify and scale technical teams.

Key Topics:
- Deconstructing the "rockstar" myth and reframing engineering errors
- Human fallibility in cybersecurity (Verizon DBIR statistics)
- Hiring barriers: degree requirements, socioeconomic bias, and irrelevant coding interviews
- Continuous on-the-job training, psychological safety, and burnout prevention

Technical Details:
Bow opens by recounting an early career incident as a security engineer at Facebook: tasked with writing a ClamAV signature to block malware on Messenger, she omitted a trailing newline in the signature file, causing the entire production antivirus scanning tier to crash and halting Messenger file uploads for over an hour. Bow highlights that the root cause was not individual incompetence, but the absence of pre-deployment linters and automated CI/CD guardrails. Citing the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR), which attributes 82% of security breaches to the human element—including configuration errors, stolen credentials, and social engineering—she argues that building resilient systems requires acknowledging that human error is inevitable, rather than expecting flawless execution from engineers.

The keynote examines the barriers exacerbating the global cybersecurity workforce deficit, estimated at over 600,000 unfilled roles. Bow critiques common job requisitions that advertise entry-level positions while demanding ten years of experience, multiple advanced certifications, and computer science degrees. Referencing an Aspen Institute study on diversity in cybersecurity, she points out that academic degrees do not reliably correlate with advanced operational competency, instead serving as socioeconomic gatekeepers that exclude high-aptitude candidates from underrepresented backgrounds. Furthermore, she condemns standard industry technical interviews that force candidates to solve irrelevant academic algorithm puzzles (such as balancing red-black binary trees) rather than assessing practical threat modeling, incident triage, or pragmatic engineering judgment.

To build sustainable security teams, Bow advocates shifting education from an upfront hiring prerequisite to an ongoing corporate employee benefit. Organizations must establish structured internal mentorship and on-the-job apprenticeship programs that train candidates who possess innate curiosity, tenacity, and problem-solving drive. She emphasizes the necessity of blameless post-mortems to foster psychological safety, allowing engineers to admit mistakes and build automated architectural safeguards. Finally, Bow addresses burnout, encouraging security professionals to actively cultivate non-technical hobbies—sharing her own background as an aerialist—to maintain perspective and mental health in a high-stress industry.

Key Takeaways:
Security leadership must eliminate arbitrary academic degree requirements and LeetCode-style algorithm tests from hiring pipelines, shifting toward practical assessments of problem-solving ability. Organizations should design engineering guardrails, linters, and blameless post-mortems that accommodate human fallibility rather than assuming developer perfection. Addressing the industry labor shortage requires treating professional education as a funded job benefit and fostering inclusive cultures that prioritize retention and burnout mitigation.

talks.title: BSidesSF 2022 - WireGuard from the ground up (Maya Kaczorowski • David Crawshaw)
talks.teaser: Presents BSidesSF 2022 - WireGuard from the ground up (Maya Kaczorowski • David Crawshaw) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
What WireGuard Is

Tailscale CTO David Crawshaw and PM Maya Kaczorowski explain WireGuard as an opinionated layer-three tunnel using modern, non-downgradable cryptography with minimal user configuration. Peers are identified by public keys—not IP addresses—supporting roaming endpoints while handling key rotation and keepalive timers automatically.

WireGuard vs TLS Mental Models

Unlike TLS client-server with certificate authorities, WireGuard is peer-to-peer: both sides must pre-share public keys (similar to SSH authorized_keys). It runs over UDP to avoid TCP-in-TCP problems, uses no fixed port, responds only to authenticated peers (reducing scanning fingerprinting), and ships as roughly 4,000 lines of kernel C versus far larger IPsec implementations.

Handshake Walkthrough

Alice and Bob each hold long-term key pairs configured ahead of time. To connect, WireGuard generates ephemeral session keys; Alice initiates by sending Bob her ephemeral public key and encrypted handshake material derived from their static keys, establishing forward-secret transport keys before encapsulating IPv4/IPv6 packets inside UDP.

talks.title: BSidesSF 2022 - An Unlikely Friendship: Why Security Engineers ... (Leif Dreizler • Rachel Landers)
talks.teaser: Details BSidesSF 2022 - An Unlikely Friendship: Why Security Engineers ... (Leif Dreizler • Rachel Landers) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Two Perspectives on Enterprise Software

Leif Dreizler, Segment/Twilio security engineering manager, and Rachel Landers, former enterprise product lead, describe friction between security engineers and product managers. Segment's customer-data platform processes trillions of events monthly for marketing and analytics customers with stringent enterprise requirements.

Product Manager Pain Points

Landers notes enterprise buyers are noisy, expensive, and demand disparate security table stakes—SSO, MFA, audit logging—that often land on product roadmaps rather than pure security teams. Complex deployments surface edge cases smaller customers never hit.

Security Engineer Pain Points

Dreizler highlights missing features, feeling disconnected from customers, difficulty proving value through metrics, and being perceived as blockers. He advocates security as a business enabler, citing industry shifts at Netflix and GitHub toward embedding security in product development like reliability or scalability.

Building Features Together

The duo shares earlier collaborations and walks through designing an enterprise security capability end to end. Their core message: intentional partnerships between product and security engineering produce customer-visible controls, better adoption, and measurable outcomes than bolt-on security work.

talks.title: BSidesSF 2022 - Detection-as-code: Why it works and where to start (Kyle Bailey)
talks.teaser: Evaluates BSidesSF 2022 - Detection-as-code: Why it works and where to start (Kyle Bailey) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Detection engineering pain points

Kyle Bailey, formerly of Box detection engineering and now at Panther Labs, argues detection-as-code treats detection logic as software products rather than one-off SIEM queries. Teams repeatedly ask when use cases ship, whether deployed logic matches what was tested, and whether new rules will flood analysts with noise.

Why code beats click-ops

Version control, peer review, CI testing, and reproducible deployments address the gap between authoring detections in a UI and reliably running them in production. Bailey emphasizes building alerts as a product for responders, with quality and maintainability as first-class goals.

Expressive languages matter

Simple IOC matching is table stakes; complex detections need imports, custom functions, and environment-specific tuning to cut false positives. Detection-as-code works across stacks when teams can express logic in full programming languages rather than limited proprietary query syntax alone.
